1:
Who the man is, and how far his affliction may be read, divides the voices at once. John Gill makes him Jeremiah, and follows one Jewish commentator in saying that his affliction exceeded that of the other prophets, who foretold the destruction but did not live to see it; he then treats the sufferer throughout as a type of Christ, taking the darkness of the second verse for the hiding of the Father’s face and the wasted flesh of the fourth for a man who at little more than thirty looked fifty. Adam Clarke allows that the prophet may speak either of himself or in the person of his countrymen, and then refuses the other reading outright: this and other passages of the poem have been applied to the passion of Christ, he says, but in his opinion without any foundation. John Calvin takes a third position. The prophet is speaking in his own person, where the earlier chapters spoke under the person of a woman, but he is not pleading a private cause; the contents show that the ode was composed for the common calamity of the whole people, and Calvin rejects as improbable the opinion that it was written while Jeremiah lay in prison.

Charles Ellicott makes the personal note the point of the whole. The lamentation is one of more intense personality than what precedes it, and for that very reason, he says, it has become the inheritance of all mourners, however far apart in time and country, whose sorrow has come near that intensity. He and Calvin notice the same silence: the wrath is plainly that of Jehovah, and yet the name is withheld, Calvin observing that the prophet speaks of him as of one well known and uses only a pronoun. Matthew Henry supplies the comfort the others leave out, that God is sometimes angry with his own people, but that this is to be complained of as a rod to correct and not as a sword to cut off, so that the anger is just and the affliction mild and mixed with mercy; and he notes that the Israel of God, though children of light, sometimes walk in darkness.

Calvin alone stops on the shape of the chapter, and does not admire it. The letters of the alphabet are tripled here, he explains, where in the earlier chapters each verse began with a successive letter, and he sets out the pattern line by line. Then he passes judgment: the verses in this chapter are needlessly multiplied, and it would have been better had each verse carried one letter, since the chapter is of the same length as the two before it.

On the darkness the voices agree and enrich each other. Clarke states the convention, that in these writings darkness stands for calamity and light for prosperity. Gill instances the captivity and the dungeon. Ellicott adds the moral sense, the darkness of perplexity as well as of misery, and matches the cry with that of Ajax in the older poet, who asked to be killed if he must be, but killed in the light. Calvin says the antithesis carries a force in Hebrew that it loses elsewhere: to say darkness and not light was to say that in that obscurity there was not so much as a spark. At the third verse Ellicott would render the clause that God turns his hand against him again and again, the first verb being one of repeated action; Gill reports a rendering that makes it only against me, as though this sufferer were the single object of it; and John Wesley reads the building of the fifth verse plainly, as forts and batteries raised against walls and houses; and Calvin takes the phrase all the day for constancy, there being no truce and no cessation, God pressing his severity without limit.
7:
The images of confinement are read at two levels, and the voices divide over which. John Gill offers the prison, the dungeon and the siege, while allowing that the words may denote the greatness of his troubles in general, like a hedge round a vineyard. Adam Clarke allows the same, that the hedging may refer to the lines drawn round the city, but adds that this and what follows may be merely metaphorical, marking a distressed condition. Charles Ellicott describes a movement in the imagery, from the darkness of the grave to that of the prison-house, where the mourner is hedged in and loaded with a heavy chain, the word being literally brass. John Calvin refuses the historical reading at the ninth verse, saying that referring the wall of hewn stone to the siege does not suit the passage; the metaphors answer to one another, life being commonly compared to a way, so that every plan the man formed was brought into straits and nothing he purposed could be carried out. Of the chain he notes that the man is not merely fettered but so weighted that he cannot lift his feet.

The eighth verse Calvin treats as the hardest thing in the passage. To cry and pray and get nothing is the extremity of all evils, he says, and it looks inconsistent, since Scripture is full of invitations to call on God, who in claiming the prerogative of hearing prayer treats it as inseparable from his own being. His answer is that God holds the faithful in suspense, and hears in such a way as to prove and try their patience, sometimes for a long while together. Ellicott states the difficulty more starkly still: the prayer is stopped so that it does not reach the ear of Jehovah, and it is Jehovah himself who stops it. Gill notes two kinds of crying, the cry wrung out by distress within and the shout for help to those outside, as prisoners cry to be heard, and that the prophet was importunate and still not heard.

On the wall of hewn stone the voices agree that the material is the point. Gill observes that it is not a hedge of thorns or a mud wall but a fence of dressed stones, cemented and set in order, and reports a paraphrase making them marble, not easily thrown down. Calvin makes the same observation from the builder’s side, that squared stones fit together and hold better than rough ones. Clarke calls them insuperable obstacles that confounded every project of deliverance. Ellicott turns it into a scene: a massive wall runs across the way, and when the traveller turns into the by-paths they twist about in labyrinthine confusion and lead nowhere. John Wesley adds the sharper point, that God not only defeated their counsels but made those counsels fatal to them.

The beasts and the archer close the passage. Gill takes the bear and the lion for the Chaldeans acting by divine permission, and the bow for all the instruments of war. Ellicott keeps to the figure and makes it consecutive: the terror of the lion turns the traveller out of his path, and there being no other path the attack follows and he is torn; and where the English says desolate he would read astonied, the verb painting the stupefaction of terror. Calvin reads the turning aside as the frustration of purpose, God directing our ways when he blesses our counsels and perverting them when nothing succeeds. Clarke sets beside the last verse an eastern saying, in which a caliph is asked where the sons of Adam could flee if heaven were a bow and earth its cord, calamities the arrows and man the butt, and God the unerring marksman; the answer was that they must flee to the Lord, and Clarke says this was exactly the case of the city.
13:
“He hath caused the arrows of his quiver to enter into my reins.” Calvin reads the line as the bow of the previous verse discharged: the arrows perforate the inward parts, so that God had dealt so severely with the people that no part, even the innermost, was sound or untouched. Gill and Clarke pause instead on the idiom. The Hebrew, Gill says, has the sons of his quiver, the quiver being compared to a pregnant woman, and he notes that Horace has a like expression. Clarke gives the rule behind it: the issue or effect, the subject, adjunct, or produce of a thing is frequently denominated its son or child, so arrows that issue from a quiver are the sons of the quiver.

The derision of the next verse divides the voices, because a man cannot well be a derision to himself. Ellicott takes the personal experience of the prophet to break through the imagery, the taunts of the mockers being the arrows that pierced to the quick. Gill records the same difficulty and reports Aben Ezra’s solution, that my people stands for peoples, the Edomites, Moabites and Ammonites who laughed at the destruction, while others refer it to the wicked among the Jews, to whom the godly were a derision. Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the word is an abbreviated plural and refuse it, the singular yielding a suitable sense here as elsewhere. Calvin answers without touching the grammar: the Prophet does not mean what was actually done, but that their state was so disgraceful that any one looking on Jerusalem might justly deride such a spectacle, and it was an equitable reward, for they had not ceased to reproach God.

Over the bitterness of the next verse the disagreement is sharper. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both note the plural, bitternesses, and the same word used of the bitter herbs eaten at the passover. Clarke observes that in almost all countries and languages bitterness is the metaphor for affliction, there being nothing more disagreeable to the taste and nothing more distressing to the mind, and he cites an Arabic poet who terms a grievously afflicted man a pounder of wormwood. Wesley glosses wormwood as severe and bitter dispensations. Calvin alone will not have the word: though wormwood is bitter, yet it is a wholesome herb, and he takes it here for poison or gall.

The figure of food is then pressed further. Ellicott says the metaphor is continued, the mourner eating bread that is gritty as if made of sand instead of flour. Gill explains the grit as bread made of corn ground with new millstones, or bread with little stones mixed in, and cites Jarchi on the breaking of the teeth. Calvin takes the image from those who press stones instead of bread under their teeth, inward and hidden griefs being like small stones. Clarke will not leave it as figure: he asks whether one can read the description without feeling the toothache, renders the second clause as a plunging into the dust, and dwells on the suffocation of eyes, ears and lungs at the first attempt to breathe. Wesley notes only that mourners were wont to throw ashes on their heads.

Peace, Calvin says, meant to the Hebrews every kind of prosperity, and the forgetting of it is not natural forgetfulness but privation, since wherever the sufferer looks around him no hope appears. Gill hears in the lost strength a lost subsistence, men who looked on themselves as of short continuance. Clarke makes hope the first and last support of the miserable, gone, and God alone able to revive it. Ellicott sees the despair as the beginning of a reaction, the very name Jehovah, no longer Adonai, reminding the mourner of the everlasting mercies.
19:
The first question is grammatical and it changes the whole posture of the verse. Gill notes that the words may be rendered imperatively, and that Aben Ezra observes they may be considered as a request to God; the prophet and his people, he adds, were not so far gone into despair as to cast off prayer, but looked up once more, beseeching God to remember them in their distressed condition. Ellicott is firmer: the verb is better taken as an imperative, the prayer addressed to Jehovah, and the mourner begins by a recapitulation of his sufferings. Calvin allows that the infinitive is often taken in Hebrew as an imperative, and that many deem it a prayer, but prefers to make the verse depend on the one before. The Prophet, he says, is excusing how he had almost fallen from hope, having been so pressed down by afflictions that his soul became as it were filled with poison and gall. Wesley says only that wormwood and gall often signify great affliction.

Calvin then turns the verse into a warning about how grief is to be handled. The faithful ought to hold a middle course in their afflictions, rousing themselves to a due consideration of their evils lest indifference and stupidity arise, but observing moderation lest sorrow swallow them up, as Paul also warns. They who fix their minds too much on the remembrance of their evils, he says, by degrees open the door to Satan, who may fill their thoughts with despair.

The next verse turns on the person of its verb. Keil and Delitzsch survey the readings that make it second person and reject them on the language: the verb means to sink down and metaphorically to be bowed down, and the sense of resting or being at ease cannot be established for it. Gill takes the second person confidently, rendering it thou wilt surely remember, and hears in it the prophet’s faith and hope increasing in prayer, that God would in much mercy remember his people and save them. Ellicott allows either and lets the received rendering stand. Calvin stays with the picture rather than the parsing: the soul is said to be humbled upon a man when he lies down under the burden of despair, and since it is the soul that raises a man up and revives him, a soul cast down upon him presses him worse than a dead body, which at least keeps its own place.

Clarke marks the hinge. In the preceding verses, he says, there is a bitterness of complaint against the bitterness of adversity that is not becoming to a man under the chastising hand of God, and while that feeling was indulged all hope fled; here he humbles himself under the mighty hand of God, and his hope revives.

What the pronoun points to divides them again. Henry says the clouds begin to disperse and the sky to clear up, that but for hope the heart would break, and that the thing recalled refers to what comes after and not to what goes before; he prefers the margin, I make to return to my heart, since what we have laid to heart is sometimes as if quite lost until God makes it return to us. Wesley agrees, taking it of what follows concerning the nature of God and his good providences. Gill points forward too, not to affliction and misery but to the abundant mercy of God and his great faithfulness. Calvin dissents: most refer the pronoun to the next verse, but a clause intervenes, so it can hardly be the meaning, and he refers it instead to the assurance already felt that God would hear. Ellicott renders it as a resolve, this will I recall, the first gleam of hope breaking through the darkness, the sorrow having brought humility, and out of humility springing hope.
22:
Ellicott begins with the architecture. It is perhaps part of the elaborate art of this poem, he says, that this section forms the centre of the book and represents the highest point of trust the mourner attains, being both preceded and followed by words of lamentation.

The first clause is disputed. The view commonly taken, Calvin allows, is that it ought to be ascribed to the mercy of God that the faithful have not been consumed, and a very useful doctrine is elicited from it, that God succors his own lest they wholly perish. But if we attend to the context, he says, another sense is more suitable: the mercies of Jehovah are themselves the subject, the particle before them being affirmative only, so that the line reads that they verily have no end, because his compassions never fail. Gill keeps the received sense and works it out at both levels. It was true of the prophet, who did not die in the dungeon, and of the people, of whom God did not make a full end but left a remnant, from whence the Messiah should come. Then he extends it: the estates of the people of God may be consumed, and their bodies by disease and death, and their peace and joy be gone for a while through temptation and desertion, but the principle of grace itself can never be lost. Clarke reads the verse as the fruit of the humbling just described. Seeing his sinfulness in a proper point of view, the sufferer finds that God has dealt with him in mercy rather than judgment, and that the affliction, excessive as it was, was less than his iniquity deserved; if any sinner is kept out of hell, Clarke adds, it is because the compassion of God fails not.

On the renewal every morning the voices converge and then Calvin qualifies. Ellicott notes that the subject is the compassions of the verse before, and that with the dawn of every day there dawn also the mercies of Jehovah. Gill calls them ever new, always fresh and vigorous, of old and yet daily renewed, making a morning of spiritual light and comfort, a morning without clouds. Clarke turns it into two questions: who could exist through the day without a continual superintending Providence, and who could be preserved in the night if the Watchman of Israel ever slumbered or slept? Calvin takes it as the morning after a night of affliction, blessings being as it were suspended during the night and renewed at dawn, and hears behind the line the psalm in which weeping dwells with us in the evening and joy returns in the morning. But the renewal, he insists, must be viewed according to the apprehension of men, for to God belongs no change; they only seem renewed when he has for a time hidden his face and again becomes reconciled to us. Wesley glosses the faithfulness as the fulfilling of promises to his people..

The portion draws out the same distinction between confession and possession. Ellicott would invert the sentence for a closer rendering, my portion is Jehovah, and traces it through the psalms to a word in Numbers. Gill sees the church rising in the exercise of faith, concluding from the mercies and the faithfulness a sure interest in God as a portion large and full, which will last for ever. Calvin makes it the only true foundation of patience: we cannot stand firm in adversity unless we are content with God alone, and there is an implied contrast, since all desire to be happy but their thoughts wander here and there. He fastens on the words saith my soul. Even the unbelieving are ashamed to deny that God is the fountain of all blessings, but confess it with the mouth only; the Prophet does not boast as hypocrites do, but speaks from a thorough persuasion.
25:
Ellicott points to the shape of the Hebrew: the alliterative form makes good the first word of three consecutive verses, predicated first of the essential character of Jehovah and then of the conditions in man on which its manifestation depends. Calvin raises the obvious objection, that adversities produce sorrow and anguish, so that those who look to God alone cannot keep hope, and answers that such confidence cannot disappoint, since the blessings by which God exhilarates his children cannot be separated from his paternal favor.

Clarke makes the waiting a matter of proportion. Hope is necessary to faith, he says, for he that hopes not cannot believe; yet hope cannot live if there be no exercise, so a man should not only wait for salvation but use every means that leads to it; and if hope become impatient faith will be impossible. Ellicott renders the phrase literally, wait in silence, abstaining from murmurs and complaints. Gill makes hope the ground of the waiting, hope being of things unseen, future, difficult and yet possible; but he guards it, that men are not to indulge a stoical apathy nor disregard the rod.

The yoke divides them. Gill offers two senses, the yoke of the commandments, as the Targum has it, or of correction, as Aben Ezra, and retains both. Calvin agrees both are admissible, then chooses: it is truly said that it is good to be accustomed from youth to the corrections of God, but the Prophet seems rather to mean obedience generally, and we bear the yoke when we relinquish our own judgment and become wise through his word. Clarke and Wesley take the harder sense. Early habits when good are invaluable and early discipline equally so, Clarke says, and he who has not got under wholesome restraint in youth will never make a useful, good, or happy man; Wesley adds that if God tame us when young, by his word or his rod, it is an unspeakable advantage. Ellicott meets a different use of the verse: the words have been pressed with a strange literalism in favour of dating the poem to the youth of Jeremiah, though the tone of the maxim is rather that of one looking back from the experience of age.

Ellicott would also change the mood of what follows, reading the next three verses as commands: let him sit alone, let him put his mouth in the dust, let him give his cheek. Calvin finds the point of the solitude in what it excludes. They who wish to appear magnanimous think their valor nothing except on a theater, while allowing themselves an unbridled liberty when alone; here we are to sit alone and be silent even were no witness present to make us ashamed.

Keil and Delitzsch derive the mouth in the dust from the custom of throwing oneself reverentially on the ground, and note that it involves humble silence, because the mouth placed in the dust cannot speak; Ellicott sees the prostration of an Eastern subject before a king. Calvin agrees that it is to become mute, the wise having nothing to say when the atrocity of evils makes his thoughts vanish; both keep the qualification that the man is not meanwhile to give up hope of deliverance. They then mark a gradation across the three verses: sitting alone in silence is the easiest, it is harder to place the mouth in the dust and yet cling to hope, and most difficult of all to give the cheek to the smiter and satiate oneself with dishonour. Calvin explains why the last is hardest. Many submit to God when they perceive his hand, in disease or famine, but when an enemy injures them they say at once that they have nothing to do with God; the patience of the godly, he insists, ought to extend to injuries of this kind, reproach being the bitterest thing.
31:
Ellicott counts the grounds of hope that follow the counsels of submission: the first, a quotation from a psalm, had of old been a favourite thought of the writer; the second rests on the fact that compassion underlies chastisement; the third on the truth that the eternal will of God is on the side of love, and that punishment is, as it were, against that will. Calvin finds the same structure in the grammar, the word for repeated three times, each clause giving a reason for the earlier saying that the Lord is good to those who wait. Gill narrows the promise before applying it: it is not of all creatures, since some are cast off for ever, but of the peculiar people of God, who may be cast down in their souls and cast out by men, yet are not cast off by God.

The next line is hard to say of God at all. Ellicott renders it literally, not from the heart, the heart being the centre of volition and emotion. Gill agrees that afflictions come from God but not from the mere motion of his heart, sin being the occasion, as Jarchi observes; God delights in mercy, while judgment is his strange act, and Wesley uses the same phrase. Clarke makes the comparison domestic: it is no pleasure to God to afflict, but like a tender parent he uses the rod, not to gratify himself but to profit and save us. Calvin alone stops to call the expression improper. God never acts unwillingly nor feignedly, and cannot be comprehended in his inconceivable glory by human minds, so he puts on our form and transfers to himself what properly applies only to men; but as parents are not willingly angry with their children, and as Christ argues from evil men who know how to do good to theirs, God never punishes except when constrained.

The three infinitives that follow can attach in two places, and the choice changes what the passage is for. Keil and Delitzsch read the whole as one sentence whose subject and predicate do not arrive until the clause about the Lord not seeing; they defend that construction against the claim that the verb never takes this preposition, disproving it from a verse in Samuel, and refer the treading down of the prisoners to the treatment of the people at the taking of Jerusalem. Gill offers both and leans to the second: either the clause continues he doth not afflict, so that God does not crush those bound in affliction and iron, or, rather, it continues the later clause, so that what God does not do he also does not approve. Calvin sets the fork out. Many join the three verses to the previous doctrine, so that God does not know what it is to pervert a good cause, since what is the nature of God but the perfection of justice; the passage is then an exhortation to patience, because the people had fully deserved what they suffered. Others take not to see as meaning not to approve, and on that reading it is a ground of consolation, God at length succoring the miserable.

Clarke reads the three clauses as a catalogue of ordinary injustice, with Blayney. The prisoners of the earth he takes for insolvent debtors put in prison and obliged to work out the debt. To turn aside the right of a man is to make him lose it because one of the higher orders opposes him, the aggravation being that it is done before the face of the Most High, in a court where God is ever considered present. To subvert a man in his cause is to prevent justice by undue interference, as by suborning witnesses. Gill follows the Targum in making the victim a poor man, which aggravates the wrong; Wesley simply counts three things which God approves not.
37:
Calvin reads the question as a rebuke of a blasphemy then prevailing everywhere, that God was content with his own leisure and exercised no care over the world. God is not a dead being, not a spectre; he is the judge of the world, and to say that anything could happen without his command was to deny his power. The following line, he adds, may be read either as a question or as a statement, with little difference in the sense.

Henry turns the truth into a duty: we must see and acknowledge the hand of God in all the calamities that befall us, personal or public. Whatever the actions of men are, God overrules them: a man devises his way, but the Lord directs his steps far otherwise than he designed, and what he contrived does not come to pass unless the counsel of God had determined it before. The Chaldeans said they would destroy Jerusalem, and it came to pass, not because they said it, but because God commanded it; men are but tools which the great God makes use of and manages as he pleases. Wesley says the same in a line, that nothing comes to pass but by the disposal of divine providence, the words being spoken in the name of the people of God, arguing themselves into quiet submission.

The word evil then has to be guarded, and Gill guards it. It stands in the plural, and is not the evil of sin or of fault, which comes not out of the mouth of God but is forbidden and condemned by him; that evil stands rather under his permissive will, which suffers it and overrules it for good. The evils meant are the judgments of God on sinners and his chastisements on his own people, of which he has determined the kind, the measure and the duration. Calvin takes the mouth to mean the decree, and notes that God does not always declare that he is a judge, having often executed punishment as it were in silence, there being no prophets among the heathens to proclaim the judgments brought upon them.

The last verse turns on a single verb. Some give it the sense of lying and others of murmuring, in neither of which Calvin can see any sense; another renders it that a man should harden himself, a mere conjecture. The verb sometimes means to weary oneself, and he takes the word used of the people in Numbers that way, Moses meaning they were wearied so that they in a manner pined away. His point is that men should not willingly weary themselves in their sins, but acknowledge that their wickedness is shown them whenever adversity comes; they would not shut God out of the government of the world if they knew themselves and called their own deeds to mind.

Clarke answers by weighing what the complainer has left. He who has his life lent to him has small cause of complaint, since however great his affliction he is still alive, and may yet find mercy unto eternal life, of which death would deprive him. Ellicott renders the clause why doth a man who lives, whose life is spared him with all its possibilities of good, complaining of sufferings which, unjust as they are on the part of those who cause them, are to the sufferer the just punishment of his own sins. Wesley hears the people checking themselves on the same ground, nothing having befallen them but the just reward of their sins. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the summons that follows and refuse one account of the transition, that instead of grumbling we should rather examine our conduct, which would turn the words into a prohibition of complaint; the real link, they say, is that our evils arise from our sins, so we are to search our faults and correct them.
40:
Ellicott marks the turn: warnings against murmurs are followed by counsels which point to a more excellent way, since suffering calls a man to self-scrutiny, and we should seek to know the sins it is meant to correct. The preposition, he notes, is emphatic, even to the Lord: there is no halting half-way in the work of conversion. Calvin sets the examination against what went before. Men weary themselves in their sins because they deplore their outward evils without considering the cause, and gain nothing but a weariness which is a sorrow to death, as Paul says, where sorrow to life proceeds from self-examination. He values the literal words, let us uncover our ways and search: the cover was first stripped off, then a search made into the character of the ways.

Clarke sets the passage out as a method for obtaining pardon. Let us examine ourselves; let us turn again to the Lord; let us lift up our heart, that is, make fervent prayer for mercy; let us lift up our hand, that is, bind ourselves in covenant to be his only, which is what lifting the hand implies, or, as some have translated the clause, let us put our heart on our hand and offer it to God; and let our confession of sin be fervent and sincere. He also pauses over the alphabet, observing that three of the verses just ahead ought, by the order of the letters, to come after the three that in fact follow them.

On the lifted hands the voices divide their labour. Ellicott renders the phrase literally, to our hands, and finds in it a psychological analysis of prayer: men can by an act of will lift up the heart as the centre of affection, which in its turn prompts the outward act of the uplifted hands, God being the final object to whom the prayer is addressed. Gill puts it the other way about: lifting up the hands is a prayer gesture and stands for prayer itself, but the heart must go with it or it is of no avail.

The confession then begins. Gill notes that the words of the prayer are not dictated but its sense directed, and that it opens as prayer should, with sin owned as a transgression of the law and as rebellion, a contempt of the authority of God, aggravated by the favours already acknowledged. Calvin would render the clause with the pronoun emphatic, we, transgressed, have we rebelled, so that the faithful take on themselves the blame of all the evils which most men sought to disown; and guilt must not be extenuated, since the most wicked are ashamed to deny that they are sinners but confess it lightly, so that the confession seems extorted and is jejune. Wesley answers the last clause in a line, that God has plagued them according to the just desert of their sins, and Keil and Delitzsch read it flatly, that God has not pardoned but positively punished. Henry is the only one who admits how mixed the passage is. It is easier to chide ourselves for complaining than to chide ourselves out of it, he says; the clouds return after the rain and the wound bleeds afresh, for great pains must be taken with a troubled spirit to bring it into temper. Calling sin a transgression and calling it a rebellion does not miscall it, and this was the fruit of searching their ways, since the more they enquired the worse they found them; but the complaint that follows carries reflections upon God which we are not to imitate. Henry calls the complaint a mistake, though a common one with the people of God when their souls are cast down: they had not the assurance and comfort of the pardon, because the judgments were not removed, and therefore thought they could not say the sin was pardoned.
43:
Calvin heads off a misreading. At first view the complaint may seem to proceed from a bitter heart, the faithful saying that they have been slain and that God executed judgment as it were in darkness without any indulgence; but it is a simple acknowledgment of righteous vengeance. Had they said they were leniently chastised it would have been very strange, for the temple had been burnt, the city demolished, the kingdom overthrown, the people driven into exile, and the covenant of God in a manner abolished.

Who is covered is disputed. Gill offers several possibilities: God covered himself, as one greatly displeased in whose face anger appears; or covered his face so as not to be seen, withdrawing his gracious presence; or, as Jarchi has it, put anger as a wall between himself and them; or, as the Targum takes it, covered his people with it. Ellicott decides for the first. Wrath, he says, is the garment in which God wraps himself to execute his judgments, and in the next verse it is represented more definitely as a cloud through which the prayers of the afflicted cannot pass. Calvin says the cloud interposed so that God might more unrestrainedly punish, and sets beside it the saying of Isaiah that the hand of God is not shortened nor his ears deaf, but that sins interposed a distance. His nature never changes; he is always ready to hear and has power to help, so that when he seems to rage the cause is to be ascribed to their sins.

On the sweepings the voices agree, and Calvin supplies the philology. The word properly means sweepings or scrapings, whatever is cleaned off a floor, and answers to the Greek term Paul uses when he says that he and his associates were the offscouring of the world. Gill says they were given into the hands of the Chaldeans to be treated as the dirt of the streets. Ellicott notes that the word rendered people is literally peoples, the heathen nations, and points to the same phrase in the apostle. Calvin adds that the degradation was open to all nations, as though God had erected a theater in Judea and exhibited there a remarkable example of his vengeance. The open mouths belong to the same picture. Gill hears lions and other beasts of prey, or else scorn poured out on their religion and the worship of God; Calvin says they had as many enemies as neighbours, that the open mouth means speaking insolently and taking the liberty of cursing, and that this was bitterest of all, since reproach grievously wounds those already afflicted.

The next line turns on two words that chime. Calvin points out the striking alliteration in the Hebrew: the people had been reduced to such straits that there was no outlet, as happens to us when we are filled with dread and see nothing but pitfalls on every side. Gill reads it as the fear of falling into the pit of ruin on whose brink they stood, and Ellicott identifies the phrase as a quotation and would render the following word devastation, the Hebrew noun occurring nowhere else though its cognate verb means to lay waste. Calvin queries a rendering of the same word: it is probably a mistake in the version of Jerome, where it is given as prophesying, and while some think he was led astray by reading a letter with the point on the wrong side, Calvin thinks the transcribers more likely committed it, desolation suiting the passage.

At the last verse the speaker turns singular. Gill notes that the prophet here speaks in his own person, expressing the anguish of his soul and his profusion of tears at the afflictions of his people. Clarke says only that he weeps incessantly; Ellicott calls it a stronger utterance of a thought already heard twice in the book.
49:
Calvin distinguishes this weeping from another kind. The unbelieving abandon themselves to sorrow but turn wholly from God and are like wild beasts; the right way to mourn is that the eyes flow without rest while we wait for God to be propitious, since otherwise tears draw us to despair, and despair becomes the cause of fury.

The next line needs parsing. Taken literally, Keil and Delitzsch say, it runs mine eye does evil to my soul, and the sense is not merely that it causes grief: the eye, weakened by incessant weeping, causes pain to the soul, the physical pain heightening that of the soul. Ellicott renders the verb harmeth, or causeth grief to. Clarke puts it plainly, that what he sees he feels, and Ellicott would render the verb of the first line poureth rather than trickleth.

Over the daughters of the city they divide. Ellicott reports two constructions, the maidens of the city or the daughter-towns that looked to it as their metropolis, and prefers the first; Clarke takes the second, the villages about Jerusalem. Calvin refuses the question by reading the preposition another way: it denotes comparison as well as cause, and the clause should run more than all the daughters of my city. Since the female sex is more tender than men, he amplifies his lamentation by claiming that in weeping he exceeded all the young women of the city, so that he had almost forgotten his manhood.

Whose sufferings these are is the larger question. Ellicott sets it out: without cause connects in the Hebrew with mine enemies, and it has been inferred that Jeremiah speaks not of the Chaldeans as enemies of his nation but of his individual persecutors, though the dungeon and the waters may be figurative here, as they are in the psalms. Clarke takes the personal reading: from here to the end of the chapter the prophet speaks of his own sufferings, especially the dungeon. Calvin takes the other side: some improperly confine this to Jeremiah himself, whereas he undertakes the cause of the whole people and encourages the faithful by his own example; Gill reads it so too. Keil and Delitzsch find a reason in the vocabulary for not narrowing it, the prophet having chosen the word for enemies rather than that for haters, lest the words be restricted to persecutions arising out of personal hatred. Calvin makes the Chaldeans fowlers and the people sparrows, there being neither prudence nor courage in birds, and alludes to the saying of Solomon that the net is spread in vain in the sight of a bird.

The stone divides them. Ellicott allows both meanings, that they cast stones at him or placed a stone over his dungeon to prevent escape. Calvin will not have the first, since stoning was not in the mind of the Prophet: a stone was laid over him that he might not come forth, as with Daniel in the den, so that the pit was like a grave. Keil and Delitzsch argue the opposite from the grammar: the verb with this preposition does not mean to cover but only to cast, and the singular for stone answers to the idiom for stoning. Wesley takes the dungeon for the lowest condition of misery. Calvin closes with a third comparison, the flood of evils, frequent in the psalms, where David set forth despair by saying he was sunk in deep waters; the words I am cut off are the saying of a man in a hopeless state, yet the Prophet was firm in hope and speaks according to the judgment of the flesh, the faithful being as it were divided, since they must be stormed by fear while faith in their hearts obtains the victory. Gill takes the waters metaphorically of affliction, and reports that Jarchi interprets them of the nations, the Chaldeans being particularly intended, whose army overflowed Judea.
55:
Henry describes the movement of the chapter. There is a struggle in the breast of the prophet between sense and faith, fear and hope: he complains and then comforts himself, yet drops his comforts and returns to his complaints; but faith gets the last word and comes off a conqueror. What comforts him is experience. They had feared that the cloud of wrath was such as their prayers could not pass through, yet find that God had not said unto them, Seek ye me in vain; when they were in the low dungeon, as free among the dead, they called upon his name. Calvin describes the same conflict inwardly, the spirit fighting against the flesh as Paul teaches. Though the Prophet apprehended death he did not cease to flee to God, the faithful not measuring the power and grace of God by their own thoughts. When Satan cannot otherwise turn us from prayer, Calvin adds, he alleges our weakness, asking whether God will hear one who trembles and despairs; against which this example should come to mind.

Ellicott says we must again choose between a literal reference to the sufferings of Jeremiah and a figurative reading, the phrase for the dungeon being the same as one in a psalm, and suggests the words may point historically to the intervention of Ebed-melech.

The breathing is disputed. Clarke takes it at its faintest: the prophet dared not complain or cry or pray aloud, but was obliged to whisper his prayer to God, and it was only a breathing. Keil and Delitzsch make it not a relaxation of oppression but a relieving of oneself by deeply drawn sighs, and render it sighing. Calvin dissents. The verb means to dilate or respire, so almost all render the noun breathing, but what follows cannot admit that sense; he takes both words for crying, since in groaning the spirit dilates and the soul, compressed by grief, expands. He also softens the petition to close not or deafen not thine ear, hiding being hardly suitable to ears.

Ellicott finds the sequence of the two clauses eminently suggestive, the recollection that prayer was answered in the past prompting its utterance in the present. Wesley says it in a line, heard in former afflictions, show me now the same favour. Calvin adds that the Prophet summons God as witness of his crying, since many boast in high terms of a fervour in prayer whose boastings are empty. Of the drawing near he says it refers to what was actually done; and though God may not speak, when we find our prayers heard it is the same as though he had said, Fear not. Clarke dwells on those two words: how powerful when spoken by the Spirit of the Lord to a disconsolate heart, so that to every mourner we may say, on the authority of God, Fear not.

The pleading of the cause is read as a legal office. Ellicott makes it the appearing of Jehovah as advocate, or next of kin protector, of the prophet in the persecutions aimed against his life; Keil and Delitzsch say the plural means not merely lawsuits but causes that concern life itself. Calvin builds on the plural too: God had contended for him not once but whenever he was in trouble, as a perpetual advocate. Friends sometimes exert themselves anxiously, interposing for our defence, but do not always succeed, whereas God is such a pleader of our cause that he is also a deliverer. At the last of these verses Calvin returns to a word. Some render it iniquity ironically, as though the Prophet said, Thou knowest whether I have offended; but the verb means to subvert, and the noun is passive, of the oppression by which his adversaries trod him down. Gill reads it so too, of the wrong done by their enemies, none of which escaped the omniscience of God.
61:
Calvin follows the turn from seeing to hearing. When God brings no aid he seems to close his eyes and render his ears deaf, but when he attends to our evils he soon brings help; and he will not let the two prepositions be flattened into one, since God had seen the purposes carried into effect against the sufferer and heard those formed concerning him. Ellicott notes that the verb governs the lips of the next verse as well as the reproaches here. On those lips he argues from the grammar: the verb properly means to meditate when no voice is uttered, but joined with lips it must mean words rather than hidden meditations, so the sense is muttering, the enemies publicly avowing what was in their hearts. He makes something of the phrase all the day: had the ungodly assaulted and soon given over it would have been easy to persevere, but their pertinacity made the trial hard, and from that he draws a ground of hope, that God will be merciful on seeing how persistent our enemies are.

Sitting and rising are read as a whole life, Ellicott saying that the two words include the daily and hourly conduct of those spoken of. Calvin distinguishes them, sitting for quiet counsels and rising for action, so that whether his enemies consulted silently or attempted this or that, nothing was unknown to God. Wesley catches the sting of the last clause, that at feasts and merry meetings the sufferer is all the subject of their discourse.

The closing petitions divide them. Gill reports that the old versions render these verses not as petitions but as prophecies, and holds that they are rather requests, that God would deal by the law of retaliation, particularly with the Chaldeans. Clarke takes the other side flatly: these are all declaratory, not imprecatory, and the line should run, thou wilt pursue them with destruction. Wesley allows both, that many passages of this nature are prophecies and some may be prophecies and prayers at once. Calvin meets the difficulty head on. Were any one to object that another rule is prescribed to us, to pray for our enemies, the answer is that the faithful in praying thus brought no violent feelings of their own but a pure zeal, rightly formed, and that the Prophet prayed for evil not indiscriminately but on the reprobate, who were perpetually the enemies of God and of his Church.

The sorrow of heart is variously read. Ellicott renders it literally covering, a veil upon the heart, signifying the blindness of obstinacy. Calvin agrees that blindness is meant, with stupidity included, and reads the request as asking God so to oppress them that they become stupefied, since it is an extremity of evil when our evils do not drive us to prayer. Gill canvasses more: a likeness between this word and the word for music, so that they who had made music of the people of God are given a doleful song of their own; and a comparison by a modern learned interpreter with an Arabic word meaning madness, which would make the sense distraction of mind.

At the last line Calvin refuses a weaker rendering. Those who make it only that God would destroy the ungodly from the earth extenuate the sentence, for the Prophet mentions the heavens of Jehovah by design, heaven being often called the throne of God; the destruction was to testify that he sits there as judge of the world, and that things are not in such confusion but that the ungodly must at length render an account. Ellicott calls the phrase exceptional but equivalent to the whole world considered as the kingdom of God. Clarke ends with the arithmetic: the chapter is a triple acrostic, three lines always beginning with the same letter, so that the Hebrew alphabet is thrice repeated, twenty-two times three being sixty-six.
